cards.title: Islamabad province?
cards.author: Aasim Sajjad Akhtar
cards.why: It addresses critical questions regarding federalism, administrative restructuring, and democratic governance in Pakistan.
cards.summary: The political establishment is reportedly considering granting Islamabad the status of a separate province. A committee led by Ahsan Iqbal has proposed a 27-member assembly for the capital. This move would further diminish the authority of the Capital Development Authority and alter the local governance structure that has persisted since 1960.
key_facts: A committee led by Ahsan Iqbal proposed an assembly of 27 members for Islamabad.
The current federal capital administration is primarily governed by the Capital Development Authority.
Islamabad has hosted only one city-wide local government election since its establishment in 1960.
The proposed structure for the new province includes an elected chief minister or mayor.

vocab.meaning: Relating to a viceroy or a system of absolute, appointed authority.
A hindrance or obstruction in doing something.

text: OPPOSITION to it has been largely suppressed, but all is not well within the ruling regime. One way or the other, the proposal to break up existing federating units will ultimately shape the regime’s endgame.

Stage one has been completed without major resistance, the PTI disarmed through the imposition of emergency in KP , and a neo-administrative experiment comprising 12 districts in the southern and ex-Fata regions operationalised.

The ultimate prize for the establishment is the long-desired separation of Karachi from the rest of Sindh. And this is where the Bhutto-Zardari clan, facing an existential threat, will be forced to play its hand.
But before this, there are likely to be other moves expected to trigger less resistance, both within the ruling coalition and outside it. One of these is the plan to make Islamabad into a province.
The bureaucracy rules Islamabad without impediment.

The only proposal on record, finalised by a committee headed by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, has advised a 27-member assembly, headed by an elected chief minister/mayor. The elephant in the room is the viceregal institution which dictates the fates of Islamabad’s three million people — the Capital Development Authority (CDA).

Pakistani democracy is, at best, an aspiration rather than a functioning reality connected to the will of the people. Elected institutions operate under pressure, while most who claim to be representatives of the people wage class war daily. Nevertheless, the pretence of democracy remains.

The federal capital is a glaring exception. The bureaucracy rules here without impediment, the popular will be damned. There has been one citywide experiment with local government since the capital was created in 1960. The 2016 elections brought the Municipal Corporation of Islamabad (MCI) into existence, under the nominal authority of an elected mayor. The mayor and elected representatives down to the level of union councillor had virtually zero legislative and financial power. Elections never took place again, and the MCI was transformed into yet another bureaucratic feeder to the CDA.

So if Islamabad is given a legislative assembly, will the CDA be cut down to size? I choose my words carefully — because those who are poised to ‘give’ Islamabad an assembly have, over the past year or so, made their plans for the city and its environs sufficiently clear.

A short list of ‘achievements’ reads as follows: thousands of homes in katchi abadis and historical villages bulldozed; suburban sprawl in the form of land-grabbing real-estate schemes extended; thousands of trees razed and the city’s air poisoned by relentless construction.

With the CDA’s Master Plan flagrantly violated by its own commercial projects and big proprietors, another post-facto amendment in zoning regulations was recently approved by the government. As for what is to come, entire chunks of Rawal Lake and many villages around Bhara Kahu will be sacrificed for a 350-acre safari park, while the area adjacent to the Bari Imam shrine — where forced evictions took place earlier this year — is being given over to hotel developers.

Will Islamabad’s much-celebrated green spaces, already limited public services, and working-class settlements be left by the time the purported legislative assembly comes into place? Will the dominant imaginary of ‘development’ fronted by the state apparatus — of which the CDA is a poster-child — suddenly give way to a political-economic-environmental arrangement that serves the mass of Islamabad’s people?

Only the awfully naïve believe that the plans for an Isla­mabad province — which may ex­­tend into adjacent districts like Mu­­rree and Haripur currently part of Punjab and KP respectively — are driven by democ­r­atic impulses. Seen thus, the Islam-abad case provides the most obvious indication of what the new provinces hullabaloo is all about; an attempt to subjugate the political and economic interests of the mass of the population, and future generations to boot, all in the name of efficient administration.

Over the course of the past year, mainstream parties like the PPP and PML-N have made no effort to stand with katchi abadi dwellers and villagers whose homes have been bulldozed in Islamabad. They have not resisted the barrage of ‘development’ projects that have forever destroyed local ecologies.

Islamabad was always the preserve of the elite, but working people fought for their rights with some success, mainstream politicians paying heed in exchange for votes. Like in the rest of the country, Islamabad’s working masses now have to exclusively wage their own political fight. They are up against both powerful elements and political entrepreneurs who hunt with the hare and run with the hound.
The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.
Published in Dawn, November 20th, 2026

cards.title: Helping create paths
cards.author: Faisal Bari
cards.why: It links constitutional obligations to socio-economic development, essential for both Pakistan Affairs and Essay papers.
cards.summary: Pakistan's education system fails to act as an equalizer, leaving children from low-income families at a severe disadvantage. While Article 25A mandates free education, the state has not provided the necessary infrastructure to bridge socio-economic gaps. A merit-based, inclusive system is essential for long-term economic growth and social cohesion.
key_facts: Article 25A of the Constitution of Pakistan guarantees the right to education.
Educational inequality is exacerbated by the lack of parental networks and poor-quality public schooling.
A merit-based education system is considered an engine for economic growth and societal harmony.

vocab.meaning: Something that makes people or situations more equal.
Having a great deal of money; wealthy.

text: ONE child, born in an affluent household, goes to one of the best private, high-fee schools, gets a lot of support from home, appears for international school leaving assessments and then makes her way to the best colleges and universities of the country or of the world. When she enters the job market, she not only has her education to bank on, and the confidence that comes with it and the upbringing she got, she has parental and university networks to support her as well.

Another child — and there are millions of children in Pakistan who face these odds — might have struggled to even be in a public or low-fee private school, is likely to drop out well before reaching college, but even if she reaches college, it is likely she will struggle to find a job afterwards. The quality of her education is compromised, she did not have much support from home for her learning, her confidence has not been built up, and she does not have a parental/family network or a university network to support her.

The state is supposed to level the playing field amongst children. Education has shown to be an amazing equaliser and the state, in theory at least, can use educational opportunities to level some of the inequalities coming from homes and families.

It is a legal and constitutional requirement in the case of basic education (Article 25A of the Constitution as well as many international commitments of our state), but it makes functional sense to do that as well: a merit-based society is likely to bring the best talent forward and that, more than anything else, becomes the engine for economic growth, social well-being and societal harmony.
The state of Pakistan has completely failed to deliver the promise of ‘the right to education’. But it has also failed, and quite miserably, to deliver on social outcomes.

Twenty-six million-odd children out of school , poor quality of education for most children enrolled in low-fee private and public schools, high dropout rate, small percentage of enrolled children reaching university level (roughly only 10 per cent), poor quality of university education in most private and public universities and very poor opportunities for employment even if you survive in the system and graduate from it with a degree.
State policies have, in many instances, helped develop & entrench inequalities.

Instead of equalising opportunities and levelling the playing field, state policies have, in many instances, helped develop and entrench inequalities even more. Funding cuts and restrictions for public education, both at school and university level, are a telling example as is the inability and unwillingness of the state to regulate provision of education by private, for-profit providers. Some effort has been made to provide scholarships, on merit, at high school and university level to help students who do well in public examinations, but, compared to the scale of poverty and the escalation in costs of education, all scholarship schemes, together, do not amount to more than a few drops in the ocean.

Private not-for-profit initiatives have also been working in the area, but the scale is a big issue here. They have been and can help hundreds of thousands, but they have not been able to reach millions. If experience from other countries is to be of value, the state has to step in and play its role.

The Citizen’s Foundation (TCF) is probably the largest non-profit provider of schooling in the country. It has been around for more than three decades and has served hundreds of thousands of students and employed thousands of teachers. But even today, TCF has less than 3,000 odd schools and school units that it runs. Pakistan has some 200,000 schools in operation in the country, and we still have 26m children out of school. How many TCFs do we need? It cannot be done without the state!

Equally important is the form of support that is provided. Even when the state has come in it has stepped in to either reduce tuition fees (public schools are free for students and public universities are still subsidised) or provide individual scholarships based on need and/or merit. But a lot more is needed. Again, if you look at examples from other countries young people need support for health and nutrition, academic support (where such support from home is missing), counselling support to ensure better career and occupation choices, scholarships, mentoring support, support for developing non-academic but needed skills in communication, self-presentation, confidence building, and support in making transition to the workplace.

These programmes, sadly, are almost completely missing in Pakistan. Even technical education, skills and training providers focus a lot more on specific skills than on issues of confidence, interpersonal skills, self-presentation and so on.

But we do need these programmes as well. Here are a couple of examples from small/local initiatives. Amal Academy does fellowships with university students to develop their skills in self-presentation, to improve confidence, to ensure better self-organisation and management. This is done over a few months through mentorship programmes that are quite structured and very interactive.

Institute of Lifelong Learning and Development, a new initiative, has a three-pronged strategy. They provide scholarships to ease access, development and mentorship programmes to focus on needed skills and confidence building and a service orientation, right from the start, to ensure benefiting students are ready to pay it forward right from the word go.

The point of these examples is to just emphasise that equalising opportunities or levelling the playing field does not get addressed through access issues (tuition fees and subsidies) only; the state needs to do a lot more. We have plenty of examples we could learn from and bodies like TEVTA and PSDF could benefit from scaling some of these programmes.

It is hard to see how Pakistan could move on the road to better human development and sustained economic growth without the state stepping in and stepping up to address some of these glaring issues of unequal opportunity sets.
The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
Published in Dawn, November 20th, 2026

cards.title: Islamic education
cards.author: Ghulam Shabbir
cards.why: It provides historical context on the evolution of intellectual traditions, relevant for understanding societal attitudes toward science and philosophy.
cards.summary: This piece explores the historical shift in Islamic education from a fusion of philosophy and science to a more rigid, orthodox approach. It argues that the rejection of rational thought and empirical science after the medieval era led to a decline in Muslim intellectual contributions. The focus on establishing formal orthodox colleges eventually overshadowed the critical philosophical inquiry of earlier centuries.
key_facts: The Nizamiyya of Baghdad was among the first orthodox colleges established for higher learning.
Imam Ghazali played a pivotal role in shaping religious thought by critiquing philosophy.
The Abbasid era witnessed both significant scientific progress and the later rise of inquisitorial boards.
The separation of religious and empirical reality was a major turning point in Islamic intellectual history.

vocab.meaning: Relating to a spiritual or non-physical realm.
Based on observation or experience rather than theory.

text: WHERE the Judeo-Christian tradition — despite its long coexistence with and exposure to Hellenism — failed at the fusion of religious and pure intellectual streams of thought, Islam sutured the fabric of transcendental and empirical reality so seamlessly that it gushed forth to spread like a prairie fire from Baghdad to India, Transoxiana and further still. The Quran so vigorously fired the imagination of Muslims and implanted philosophic spirit in them that within a short time they mastered the sciences and were at the helm of world affairs.

However, orthodox elements blew this fusion of metaphysical and social reality into shreds and after a few centuries, the real ‘dark ages’ of Muslims set in. The clergy was left with little more than a threadbare formal structure of ideas. How did things come to such a pass?

It was a protracted war between orthodox elements and philosophers, fought from rigid positions which shaped the content of Islamic education and Muslim attitude towards philosophy and positive sciences, of which both Muslim thought and philosophy paid the price. The capture of Bait al-Hikma at Baghdad by the Mu’tazila, with an Abbasid inquisition board, was a shot across the bow to the ulema to make them realise how vital an education system is to state and society. So they set about to organise and control education. Thus, Nizamiyya Baghdad was the first orthodox college of higher learning where Ghazali served as professor. At almost the same time occurred the philosophical movement, which was critical of religion.

Ghazali saved religious thought from the critique of philosophers, but his wholesale rejection of philosophy and positive sciences proved a watershed event for later developments, as his community took his statements as ‘eternal truth’ rather than an overreaction to an extreme historical challenge.
Both philosophers and orthodoxy failed to mediate their rigidity.

However, he failed to appreciate that no structure of ideas can survive without constant interaction with a living and growing stream of positive and scientific thought, and banishment of positive sciences can deal a deadly blow to knowledge as an organic whole.

Ibn Khaldun warned philosophers that the balance (intellect), meant to weigh gold, cannot weigh down mountains and told orthodoxy that ulema severed from Sitz im leben and social realities cannot be the real successors of the Prophet (PBUH). In a nutshell, both philosophers and orthodoxy failed to mediate their rigidity and went off a cliff. So, where philosophers outraged theology by interpreting the Quran through the lens of Hellenistic thought, orthodoxy proscribed philosophy, positive sciences and their instrument, human reason. Free thought, by its very nature, is bound to exceed on certain points, but its remedy is not to stifle it but to keep on criticising it to reach a balanced conclusion.

However, rise of philosophy in Islam was sporadic and individual. It never took the form of a movement or a tradition of enduring roots, as was the case in ancient Greece and the modern West. Confined to theological problems, the Mu’tazila’s rationalism was not purely philosophical as the fulcrum of their thought was to know whether free will was compatible with the idea of a Just God. Muslim philosophers were too enamoured of metaphysical heights to climb down to ethics. Had they made Sharia an object of study, the subsequent history of philosophy and Islamic thought could have been different.

Thus, since orthodoxy’s triumph against philosophy, Ghazali has been leading the fleets of Islamic thought to harbour on theological rather than Archimedean principles. Ibn al-Arabi extended his premises to supplant reason with Sufi intuition. Ibn Taimiyya’s attacks against philosophy are well-known. Al-Shatibi discourages the cultivation of purely in­­tellectual disciplines since they are not related to action and denies the role of reason in formulation of law and moral imperatives, though he himself employs a generous quantum of reason in his constructs. Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi unreservedly ridicules and rejects positive sciences.

Thus, madressah education, arguably since its very inception, was destined to culminate in intellectual barrenness. The panacea lies in an organic fusion of traditional learning and modern ethos, but given the reforms at Deoband, al-Azhar and Zaituna, the ulema manoeuvred juxtaposition of the two rather than synthesis of the old and the new. The long-quarantined religious knowledge gets fossilised and an unalterable law of God is that fossils do not survive long. As it is stated in the Holy Quran, “…We did not do them injustice; but they were unjust to themselves. …” (11:101). Are Muslims ready to reform Islamic education, or are they waiting for a Luther?
The writer is an academic.
Published in Dawn, November 20th, 2026

cards.title: The mystery of silence
cards.author: Naween A. Mangi
cards.why: It illustrates common governance failures, such as opacity and lack of professional communication in public departments.
cards.summary: The author highlights the inefficiency and lack of accountability within government departments using the Sindh Culture Department as a case study. Attempts to secure access to public venues for cultural events were met with evasion and ghosting from officials. The essay critiques the necessity of 'string-pulling' to bypass bureaucratic obstacles.
key_facts: Public cultural spaces in Sindh are often inaccessible for independent theatre or art productions.
Bureaucratic culture frequently relies on evasion and false assurances rather than clear official responses.
Personal influence and 'string-pulling' remain significant factors in accessing public services.

vocab.meaning: The act of avoiding something, often a duty or a direct answer.
Firmly established and difficult to change.
